decks.title: Money and Inflation — Part 1: Meaning, Kinds and Functions of Money
goals: Explain the difficulties of barter and the meaning of money
Distinguish the kinds of money, legal tender, fiat money and near money
Explain the primary, secondary and contingent functions of money with examples

slides.heading: Money: Meaning, Kinds and Functions
slides.body_md: Part 1 — why **barter** fails, what **money** is, its **kinds**, and the **functions** it performs.

visual.alt: Flow of the evolution of money: barter, commodity money such as grain or salt, metallic coins, paper money and bank or credit money
visual.caption: How money evolved

slides.narration: Imagine trying to buy a notebook by offering the shopkeeper a bag of potatoes. It would rarely work. In this part we see why such exchanges are so hard, how money grew from grain and coins to notes and bank deposits, what kinds of money exist today, and the many jobs that money does for us.

slides.heading: The difficulties of barter
slides.body_md: Under **barter**, goods are swapped directly for goods. Trade is slow and often impossible.

rows: The potter wants rice; the rice grower wants sandals, not pots
How many pots equal one goat? A new rate for every swap
A goat cannot be split to buy a small sack of salt
Fish and vegetables rot before they can be traded
A loan of rice repaid in rice may differ in quality

visual.alt: Table of five difficulties of barter with examples from an imagined village market: double coincidence of wants, no common measure of value, indivisibility of goods, no store of value and no standard of deferred payment

slides.narration: Barter means swapping goods directly. The biggest problem is that both sides must want exactly what the other has. There is also no common unit to measure value, many goods cannot be divided, perishable goods cannot be stored, and loans cannot be repaid fairly. Money solves all these problems.

slides.heading: Meaning of money
slides.body_md: **Money** is anything that is **generally accepted** as a means of payment for goods and services and in settlement of debts.

visual.alt: Flow of the evolution of money: barter, commodity money such as grain or salt, metallic coins, paper money and bank or credit money
visual.caption: How money evolved

slides.narration: Money is defined by what it does, not by what it is made of. Anything that people generally accept in payment, and in settling debts, can serve as money. Over time societies used grain and salt, then metal coins, then paper notes, and now deposits that move between bank accounts.

slides.heading: Kinds of money: from commodities to bank money
slides.body_md: **Commodity**, **metallic** (full-bodied or token), **paper** and **credit (bank)** money.

rows: A useful good accepted in payment
Salt bars used to buy cloth
An old silver coin worth its silver
A ₹5 coin with metal worth far less
Notes issued by the monetary authority
Deposits moved by cheque or transfer
A trader paying a supplier by cheque

visual.alt: Table of kinds of money with meanings and imagined examples: commodity money, full-bodied coins, token coins, paper money and credit or bank money

slides.narration: Commodity money is a useful good used in payment. Metallic money is coins; a full-bodied coin contains metal worth its face value, while a token coin is worth more as money than as metal. Paper money is notes issued by the monetary authority. Credit or bank money is deposits that move by cheque or transfer.

slides.heading: Legal tender, fiat money and optional money
slides.body_md: **Legal tender** must be accepted in payment of debts; **fiat money** gets its value from government order; **cheques** are optional money.

rows: Must be accepted for any amount
Must be accepted only up to a legal limit
Money by government order; value not from its material

visual.alt: Table of legal tender terms: unlimited legal tender such as notes, limited legal tender such as small coins, optional money such as cheques, and fiat money issued by government order

slides.narration: Legal tender is money that the law says must be accepted in payment. Notes are unlimited legal tender, while small coins are limited legal tender, accepted only up to a legal limit. Fiat money has value because the government orders it, not because of its material. A cheque is optional money: a seller may refuse it.

slides.heading: Quick check: a bag of coins
slides.body_md: A customer tries to pay a large bill entirely in small coins. The baker refuses beyond a limit. The coins are…
slides.narration: Think about what the law says must be accepted, and up to what amount.

slides.heading: Money and near money
slides.body_md: **Near money** is a highly liquid asset that can quickly be turned into cash but **cannot itself pay** for goods.

rows: Used directly to pay for goods?
High, but must first be turned into cash

visual.alt: Table comparing money and near money: money pays for goods directly and is perfectly liquid; near money such as a fixed deposit or treasury bill is highly liquid but must first be converted into cash

slides.narration: Some assets are almost as good as money. A fixed deposit, a treasury bill or a bond can be turned into cash quickly and with little loss. But you cannot hand a fixed deposit to a shopkeeper in payment. Such assets are called near money.

slides.heading: Quick check: near money
slides.body_md: Which asset of an imagined Chennai family is near money?
slides.narration: Ask of each asset: could the family pay for groceries with it directly?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: classifying a family's holdings
slides.body_md: An imagined family in Bhopal holds cash, a current account, a fixed deposit and a treasury bill.
bullets: Step 1 — Ask: can it be used **directly** to pay?
Step 2 — If yes, it is **money**; if it must first be converted, it is **near money**.
Step 3 — Give the reason in each case.

headers: Holding of an imagined Bhopal family

visual.alt: Table classifying four holdings of an imagined family: cash and a current-account balance are money; a fixed deposit and a treasury bill are near money

slides.narration: Apply one test to each holding. Cash and a current-account balance can be used to pay at once, so they are money. A fixed deposit must first be withdrawn and a treasury bill must first be sold, so both are near money. Always write the reason, because that is where the marks are.

slides.body_md: Functions fall into **three groups**: primary, secondary and contingent.

visual.caption: Three groups of functions, as classified for ISC.

slides.narration: Economists group the work that money does into three sets. The primary functions are the basic ones every money must perform. The secondary functions grow out of them. The contingent functions arise in a developed economy with banks and markets. Let us take each group in turn.

slides.heading: Primary functions
slides.body_md: **Medium of exchange** and **measure (unit) of value**.

rows: Splits a swap into a sale and a purchase
A weaver sells a saree, then buys yarn
Expresses all values in one unit
A dairy records milk, fodder and wages in rupees

visual.alt: Table of the two primary functions of money: medium of exchange, which splits a swap into a sale and a purchase, and measure of value, which expresses all values in one unit

slides.narration: As a medium of exchange, money splits a barter swap into two separate deals: you sell for money to one person and buy with money from another. As a measure of value, money gives every good a price in one unit, the rupee, so that values can be compared and added up.

slides.heading: Secondary functions
slides.body_md: **Standard of deferred payments**, **store of value** and **transfer of value**.

rows: A seed loan repaid in rupees after harvest
A vendor saves money, not tomatoes
Moves purchasing power between places or people
Selling a house in Bihar to buy a flat in Bengaluru

visual.alt: Table of the three secondary functions of money: standard of deferred payments, store of value and transfer of value, with imagined examples

slides.narration: Because money measures value, future payments such as loans can be fixed in it: that is the standard of deferred payments. Money can also be saved and used later, which makes it a store of value. And it lets people move purchasing power from one place or person to another, called transfer of value.

slides.heading: Quick check: saving for later
slides.body_md: Keeping part of today's income as money to spend later uses money as a ___ of value.
slides.narration: Which word describes holding purchasing power for the future?

slides.heading: Contingent functions
slides.body_md: Functions that depend on a developed money economy: **credit**, **income distribution**, **liquidity** and **solvency**.

rows: Loans and deposits are claims to money
Output is shared as wages, rent, interest and profit in money
Spending can be spread so each rupee gives similar satisfaction
Money is the most liquid asset
Holding money shows ability to pay debts

visual.alt: Table of contingent functions of money: basis of credit, distribution of national income, equalising marginal utilities, liquidity and guarantor of solvency

slides.narration: Contingent functions appear once an economy has banks and markets. Money is the base on which credit is built. It allows national income to be shared out as wages, rent, interest and profit. It is the most liquid asset, and holding it shows that a person or firm can pay its debts.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: one day at a dairy cooperative
slides.body_md: Match each event at an imagined dairy in Anand with the function of money it shows.

headers: Event at an imagined Anand dairy
rows: Milk bought from members at a price per litre in rupees
Members paid in cash every ten days
Loan for a chilling plant repaid over five years
Surplus kept in the bank for the next drought
Bank lends to the dairy against its deposits

visual.alt: Worked example table matching five events at an imagined dairy to functions of money: pricing milk is a measure of value, paying members is a medium of exchange, repaying a loan is a standard of deferred payments, keeping a surplus is a store of value and a bank loan shows money as the basis of credit

slides.narration: Here is a day at an imagined dairy. Paying a price per litre uses money as a measure of value. Paying members in cash makes it a medium of exchange. Repaying a loan over five years uses it as a standard of deferred payments. A surplus kept for a drought is a store of value, and a bank loan shows money as the basis of credit.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Anything generally accepted in payment for goods and debts
Commodity, metallic (full-bodied, token), paper, credit; legal tender, fiat, near money
Medium of exchange; measure of value
Deferred payments; store of value; transfer of value
Basis of credit; distributing income; liquidity; solvency

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: meaning of money, its kinds, and its primary, secondary and contingent functions

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. Money is whatever is generally accepted in payment. It comes in several kinds, from commodities and coins to notes and bank deposits, and the law decides what is legal tender. Money performs two primary functions, three secondary functions and several contingent functions in a modern economy.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Define money by **general acceptability**, not by its material.
Name the **group** of each function: primary, secondary or contingent.
For a scenario, **identify** the function or kind of money, then **explain** it in one line from the scenario.
Distinguish **legal tender** from **optional money**, and **money** from **near money**.

rows: "A cheque is money that must be accepted"
A cheque is optional money; only legal tender must be accepted
Listing store of value as a primary function

visual.alt: Table of common mistakes in Part 1 with corrections: cheques are optional money, fixed deposits are near money, and store of value is a secondary function

slides.narration: In the exam, define money by acceptance, not by what it is made of. When asked about functions, say which group each belongs to. In scenario questions, first name the function or kind of money, then explain it using words from the scenario. And keep legal tender, optional money and near money clearly apart.

decks.title: Money and Inflation — Part 2: Money Supply and Inflation
goals: Explain the meaning of money supply and of the measures M0, M1, M2, M3 and M4
Explain inflation and calculate the rate of inflation and the purchasing power of money from a price index
Explain demand-pull and cost-push inflation and their causes

slides.heading: Money Supply and Inflation
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how **money supply** is measured, and what happens when prices keep **rising**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: money supply, reserve money, narrow and broad money, inflation, and demand-pull and cost-push inflation
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: How much money is there in an economy, and what happens when prices keep rising? In this part we learn how the central bank measures the stock of money, from the narrowest measure to the broadest. Then we study inflation: what it means, how to measure it from a price index, and its two main causes.

slides.heading: Meaning of money supply
slides.body_md: **Money supply** is the **stock** of money held by the **public** at a point of time.

nodes.label: Held by the public (households and firms)
Excludes government and banks' own cash

visual.alt: Flow describing money supply: the stock of money held by the public at a point of time, excluding money held by the government and the banking system
visual.caption: Money supply: meaning

slides.narration: Money supply is a stock, measured at a point of time, not a flow over a period. It counts only money held by the public, meaning households and firms. Cash lying with the government or in banks' own vaults is left out, because it is not available to the public for spending.

slides.heading: Reserve money
slides.body_md: **M0 (reserve money)** = currency in circulation + bankers' deposits with the RBI + other deposits with the RBI.

rows: Notes and coins with the public and in bank tills
Banks' reserves kept with the central bank
Deposits of some institutions with the central bank

visual.alt: Table of the components of reserve money: currency in circulation, bankers' deposits with the central bank and other deposits with the central bank
visual.caption: Also called high-powered money: the base for bank credit.

slides.narration: Reserve money is the base of the money system. It includes all currency in circulation, the deposits that banks keep with the central bank, and some other deposits with the central bank. It is called high-powered money because banks create many times this amount as deposits.

slides.heading: Measures of money supply
slides.body_md: Narrow money: **M1**, **M2**. Broad money: **M3**, **M4**.

rows: Currency with the public + demand deposits of banks + other deposits with the RBI
M1 + savings deposits with post office savings banks
M1 + net time deposits of banks
M3 + total deposits with the post office savings organisation (excluding National Savings Certificates)

visual.alt: Table of money-supply measures: M1 is currency with the public plus demand deposits plus other deposits with the central bank; M2 adds post office savings bank deposits; M3 adds net time deposits of banks to M1; M4 adds total post office savings deposits to M3; M1 and M2 are narrow money, M3 and M4 broad money
visual.caption: Classic RBI measures as studied for ISC; meanings only.

slides.narration: Narrow money counts currency with the public, demand deposits and other deposits with the central bank. The next measure adds post office savings bank deposits. Broad money adds the time deposits of banks, and the broadest measure also adds total post office savings deposits. We only need their meanings, not calculations.

slides.narration: This sketch shows order only. The narrowest measure contains the most liquid forms of money, which can be spent at once. Each broader measure adds savings and time deposits that take longer to use. So liquidity falls as we move from narrow money to broad money.

slides.heading: Inflation and how it is measured
slides.body_md: **Inflation** is a **sustained rise in the general price level**; it is measured with a **price index**.

rows: A sustained rise in the general price level
Cost of a fixed basket now ÷ cost in the base year × 100
(Index this year − index last year) ÷ index last year × 100

visual.alt: Table defining inflation, a price index, the rate of inflation and the purchasing power of a rupee

slides.narration: Inflation is not one price going up once. It is a lasting rise in the general level of prices. We measure it with a price index, which compares the cost of a fixed basket of goods with its cost in a base year. When the index rises, each rupee buys less.

slides.body_md: Rate of inflation = (index this year − index last year) ÷ index last year × 100.
bullets: The rate itself is rising: prices climb faster each year.

slides.heading: Demand-pull inflation
slides.body_md: Prices are **pulled up** when aggregate demand exceeds what the economy can produce at full employment.

nodes.label: More money supply, public spending or income
Economy at full employment: output cannot rise

visual.alt: Flow of demand-pull inflation: more money supply, public spending or income raises aggregate demand; at full employment output cannot rise, so prices are pulled up
visual.caption: Demand-pull inflation (no diagram required)

slides.narration: Demand-pull inflation begins with spending. More money supply, higher government spending, a tax cut or rising exports all raise aggregate demand. If the economy is already at full employment, output cannot rise to meet it, so buyers compete for the same goods and prices are pulled up.

slides.heading: Cost-push inflation
slides.body_md: Prices are **pushed up** when the **cost of production** rises, even if demand has not.

Prices pushed up without more demand

slides.narration: Cost-push inflation begins with costs. If wages rise faster than productivity, if imported fuel or raw materials become dearer, if powerful firms widen their margins, or if indirect taxes rise, the cost of each unit goes up. Firms pass these costs on as higher prices, even though demand has not grown.

sections.heading: 1. From barter to money
sections.body_md:
- **Barter** is the direct swapping of goods. Its difficulties: need for a **double coincidence of wants**; **no common measure of value**; **indivisibility** of goods; **no store of value** for perishables; **no fair standard** for future payments.
- **Money** is anything **generally accepted** in payment for goods and services and in settling debts.
- Money evolved from **commodities** (grain, cattle, salt) to **metal coins**, **paper notes** and **bank deposits**.

sections.heading: 2. Kinds of money
sections.body_md:
- **Commodity money**: a useful good used in payment.
- **Metallic money**: **full-bodied** coins (metal worth = face value) and **token** coins (face value above metal worth).
- **Paper money**: notes; modern notes are **inconvertible** (not exchangeable for gold on demand).
- **Credit (bank) money**: deposits moved by cheque or transfer.
- **Legal tender**: must be accepted in payment of debts — **unlimited** (notes) or **limited** (small coins, up to a legal limit). Cheques are **optional money**.
- **Fiat money**: issued by government order; value does not come from its material.
- **Near money**: highly liquid assets (fixed deposits, treasury bills, bonds) that must first be turned into money.

sections.heading: 3. Functions of money
sections.body_md:
- **Primary**: **medium of exchange** (sale and purchase become separate deals); **measure of value** (common unit of account).
- **Secondary**: **standard of deferred payments** (loans fixed in money); **store of value** (purchasing power kept for later — weakened when prices rise fast); **transfer of value** (between places and people).
- **Contingent**: **basis of credit**; **distribution of national income** as wages, rent, interest and profit; **equalising marginal utilities** in spending; **liquidity**; **guarantor of solvency**.

sections.heading: 4. Money supply: M0 to M4 (meanings)
sections.body_md:
- **Money supply**: the **stock** of money held by the **public** at a point of time; money with the government and the banking system is excluded.
- **M0 (reserve or high-powered money)** = currency in circulation + bankers' deposits with the RBI + other deposits with the RBI.
- **M1** = currency with the public + demand deposits of banks + other deposits with the RBI.
- **M2** = M1 + savings deposits with post office savings banks.
- **M3** = M1 + net time deposits of banks.
- **M4** = M3 + total deposits with the post office savings organisation (excluding National Savings Certificates).
- **M1, M2**: narrow money; **M3, M4**: broad money. Liquidity is highest in M1 and lowest in M4.

sections.heading: 5. Inflation and its measurement
sections.body_md:
- **Inflation**: a **sustained rise in the general price level**, so money loses **purchasing power**.
- **Price index** = cost of a fixed basket now ÷ cost in the base year × 100.
- **Rate of inflation** = (rise in the index) ÷ (earlier index) × 100.
- **Purchasing power of ₹1** = 100 ÷ price index; **real value** of an amount = amount × 100 ÷ index.
- Imagined Sonapur: 125 → 135 → 148.5 gives 8% and then 10%; a rupee at index 125 buys ₹0.8 of base-year goods.
- Imagined Meghpur: a basket costing ₹4,000 now costs ₹4,600 (index 115, a 15% rise); a salary of ₹46,000 is worth ₹40,000 in base-year rupees.

key_terms.definition_md: A sustained rise in the general level of prices.

sections.heading: 6. Demand-pull and cost-push inflation
sections.body_md:
- **Demand-pull**: aggregate demand exceeds full-employment output. Causes: rise in **money supply** and easy credit, higher **public spending** (especially **deficit financing**), higher **disposable income** (tax cuts), rising **exports**, growing population.
- **Cost-push**: rising **costs** raise prices without more demand. Types: **wage-push**, **profit-push**, dearer **inputs or imports** (fuel, raw materials), higher **indirect taxes**.
- Demand-pull usually appears at full employment; cost-push can appear with idle capacity and may reduce output.
- *Diagrams of both types are not required for ISC 2027; explain them in words.*

questions.stem_md: In an imagined hill village with no money, a potter wants rice but the only rice grower nearby wants a pair of sandals, not pots. Which difficulty of barter does this show?

options.text_md: Lack of a common measure of value
Lack of double coincidence of wants

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Lack of double coincidence of wants. An exchange needs each party to want exactly what the other offers. Here the grower does not want pots, so the wants do not coincide. The other options are also barter problems, but not the one described.

questions.stem_md: A shopkeeper in an imagined Kanpur market refuses a customer's cheque but cannot lawfully refuse a valid currency note in settlement of a debt. This is because the currency note is

options.text_md: near money, while a cheque is legal tender
commodity money, while a cheque is fiat money
full-bodied money, while a cheque is token money
legal tender, while a cheque is optional (non-legal-tender) money

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** legal tender, while a cheque is optional (non-legal-tender) money. Currency notes issued under the authority of law must be accepted in payment of a debt; a cheque is credit money that the receiver may accept or refuse.

questions.stem_md: A ₹10 coin in an imagined coin exhibition at Hyderabad contains metal worth far less than ten rupees. Such a coin is called
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** token money. A token coin has a face value higher than the value of the metal in it. A full-bodied coin has metal worth its face value; commodity money is a good used as money; near money is not a medium of exchange at all.

questions.stem_md: Ravi, a trader in an imagined Surat textile market, settles most bills by cheque drawn on his current account. The money he uses is best described as

options.text_md: fiat money issued by the government

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** credit (bank) money. Demand deposits that are transferred by cheque are created and held by banks; they are credit or bank money. They are not a commodity, not coins and not government-issued notes.

questions.stem_md: A customer at an imagined Pune bakery tries to pay a large bill entirely in small coins, and the baker refuses beyond a limit. The coins are an example of
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** limited legal tender. Limited legal tender must be accepted only up to a limit fixed by law; beyond it the receiver may refuse. Currency notes are unlimited legal tender.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following assets held by an imagined Chennai family is near money rather than money?

options.text_md: A fixed (time) deposit in a bank
Currency notes in the household cash box
Balance in a savings-cum-current account usable by cheque

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A fixed (time) deposit in a bank. A time deposit can be turned into money quickly with little loss, but it cannot itself be used to pay for goods. Currency, coins and chequable deposits are money.

questions.stem_md: A museum guide in an imagined Kolkata gallery says that modern currency notes are "inconvertible paper money". This means the notes

options.text_md: can be exchanged for gold of equal value on demand
are accepted only within one state
have metal content equal to their face value
cannot be exchanged for gold or silver on demand at the issuing authority

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** cannot be exchanged for gold or silver on demand at the issuing authority. Inconvertible paper money is not backed by a promise to pay gold or silver; it is accepted because the law makes it legal tender. Convertible paper money once promised such exchange.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined island trading story, cowrie shells and salt bars were accepted in payment for all goods. Such money is called
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** commodity money. When a useful good itself serves as the generally accepted means of payment, it is commodity money.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A currency note of an imagined country is accepted in payment even though the paper itself is almost worthless.

**Reason (R):** Fiat money derives its value from the order of the government that makes it legal tender, not from the material it is made of.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: people accept fiat money because the law makes it legal tender and others accept it, not because of the value of the paper.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Money removes the need for a double coincidence of wants.

**Reason (R):** Money is a durable asset that can be kept for future use.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true. But A is explained by money acting as a medium of exchange (sell to anyone for money, buy from anyone with money), not by its durability, so R is not the correct explanation.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A seller in an imagined Indore wholesale market must, by law, accept a cheque offered in payment, because a cheque is legal tender.
questions.solution_md: **False.** A cheque is not legal tender. It is an order to a bank to pay from a deposit, so the seller may refuse it; only legal tender must be accepted in settlement of a debt.

questions.stem_md: Match each example from an imagined money museum in Nagpur with the kind of money it shows.

options.text_md: Bars of salt used to buy cloth
A coin whose metal is worth less than its face value
A bank deposit transferred by cheque
A treasury bill held by a firm

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Salt bars are a good used as money; the coin's face value exceeds its metal value; a chequable deposit is bank money; a treasury bill is a liquid asset that is not itself a medium of exchange.

questions.stem_md: State two difficulties that an imagined weekly haat in rural Odisha would face if it ran on barter instead of money.
questions.solution_md: Any two barter problems, each explained briefly.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Double coincidence of wants**: a seller must find a buyer who has exactly what the seller wants in return.
2. **No common measure of value**: the rate of a goat in terms of rice, cloth or pots has to be fixed afresh for every exchange.

questions.stem_md: What is near money? Give one example from the savings of an imagined Lucknow household.
questions.solution_md: Meaning with the liquidity point; one example.

answer.model_answer_md: **Near money** is an asset that can be turned into money **quickly and with little loss**, but cannot itself be used to **pay for goods**. Example: the household's **fixed deposit** in a bank or its **treasury bills**.

questions.stem_md: Explain fiat money, and say why people in an imagined country accept fiat notes that have almost no material value.
questions.solution_md: Meaning and the basis of acceptance.

answer.model_answer_md: **Fiat money** is money issued **by order of the government**, whose value does not depend on the material it is made of. People accept it because the **law makes it legal tender** and they are confident that **others will accept it** in turn.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between limited and unlimited legal tender with one example of each, as a cashier at an imagined Jaipur bank would explain it.
questions.solution_md: Both terms with an example each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Unlimited legal tender** must be accepted in payment of **any amount**, for example **currency notes**. **Limited legal tender** must be accepted only **up to a limit fixed by law**, beyond which it may be refused, for example **small coins**.

questions.stem_md: A group of fishermen in an imagined coastal village of Kerala want to buy rice, pay a carpenter next season and save for a boat. Explain three difficulties they would face under barter.
questions.solution_md: Three difficulties, each tied to a need in the stem.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Double coincidence of wants**: the rice seller may not want fish, so the exchange fails.
2. **No standard of deferred payment**: a promise to pay the carpenter "in fish next season" is risky, since fish vary in quality and value.
3. **No store of value**: fish are **perishable**, so the fishermen cannot store their wealth in fish to buy a boat later.

questions.stem_md: A firm in an imagined Ludhiana industrial area holds cash, a current-account deposit and a three-year bond. Classify each as money or near money, giving reasons.
questions.solution_md: Each asset classified with the reason (medium of exchange or not).

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Cash** is **money**: it is legal tender and can be spent at once.
2. The **current-account deposit** is **money** (credit money): it can be **used to pay** by cheque or transfer.
3. The **three-year bond** is **near money**: it can be **sold for cash** fairly quickly, but it **cannot itself be used to pay** for goods.

questions.stem_md:
An imagined school museum in Bhopal is labelling its money gallery.

(a) Explain commodity money and metallic money, distinguishing full-bodied from token coins. [3]
(b) Explain the difference between legal tender and fiat money on the one hand and credit money on the other. [2]
questions.solution_md: Commodity and metallic money, full-bodied versus token; legal tender and fiat versus credit money.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Commodity money** is a useful good, such as grain, cattle or salt, that is generally accepted in payment. **Metallic money** is coins of metal. A **full-bodied coin** has metal worth its **face value**, so melting it loses nothing; a **token coin** has a face value **higher** than its metal value, as with modern coins.
(b) **Legal tender** must be accepted in payment of debts by law, and **fiat money** is issued **by order of the government**, with value that does not depend on its material; modern notes are both. **Credit money**, such as a bank deposit transferred by **cheque**, is created by banks and is **optional**: a seller may refuse it.

questions.stem_md:
An imagined tribal cooperative in Chhattisgarh moves from swapping forest produce to selling it for money.

(a) Explain three problems of barter that this change removes. [3]
(b) Explain how money, as a measure of value, helps the cooperative keep accounts. [2]
questions.solution_md: Three barter problems linked to the cooperative; accounts in a common unit.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) 1. **Double coincidence of wants**: members can sell honey to anyone for money and buy rice from anyone else.
2. **No common measure of value**: every swap needed a new rate (honey for rice, honey for cloth); money gives **one price** for each good.
3. **Indivisibility**: a member with one bag of tamarind could not "split" it to buy small items; money comes in **small units**.
(b) With money as a **unit of account**, sales, costs and members' shares can be **added up in rupees**. The cooperative can compare income with expenses, calculate **profit** and pay each member a fair share.

questions.stem_md: A weaver in an imagined Varanasi lane sells a saree for money and later uses the money to buy yarn from a different trader. Which function of money is at work?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Medium of exchange. Money is accepted in the sale and passed on in a purchase: it splits one barter into two separate exchanges. That is its role as a medium of exchange.

questions.stem_md: A dairy cooperative in an imagined Anand village records the value of milk, fodder and wages in rupees so that they can be added and compared. Which function of money does this show?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Measure (unit) of value. Expressing different goods in one unit, the rupee, so they can be compared and added is the measure-of-value (unit-of-account) function.

questions.stem_md: A farmer in an imagined Vidarbha village borrows ₹20,000 for seeds and promises to repay in rupees after the harvest. Which function of money makes such a contract easy?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Standard of deferred payments. Future payments, such as loan repayments, are fixed in money; this is money acting as a standard of deferred payments.

questions.stem_md: Meera sells her house in an imagined town in Bihar and buys a flat in Bengaluru with the money. Which function of money has she used?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Transfer of value. Money lets a person move purchasing power from one place (or person) to another, which is the transfer-of-value function.

questions.stem_md: A bank in an imagined Mysuru branch can lend many times its cash reserves because people trust that deposits are claims to money. This shows money acting as

options.text_md: a medium of exchange, a primary function
a measure of value, a primary function
a store of value, a secondary function
the basis of the credit system, a contingent function

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the basis of the credit system, a contingent function. Credit is built on money: deposits and loans are promises to pay money. Being the basis of credit is a contingent function.

**Reason (R):** When the general price level rises, each unit of money buys fewer goods.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.

questions.solution_md: Store-of-value function contrasted with a perishable good.

answer.model_answer_md: Money is a better **store of value**: tomatoes are **perishable** and lose value in days, while money keeps its value (when prices are stable), is easy to **keep and carry**, and can be spent on **anything** later.

questions.stem_md: Name the two primary functions and any two secondary functions of money, as a revision list for an imagined Patna commerce class.
questions.solution_md: Two primary and two secondary functions.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Primary functions**: **medium of exchange** and **measure (unit) of value**.
**Secondary functions**: any two of **standard of deferred payments**, **store of value** and **transfer of value**.

questions.stem_md: An imagined cycle-repair shop in Agra (i) prices repairs in rupees, (ii) is paid in cash by customers and (iii) sells spare parts on credit to be paid next month. Identify the function of money in each case and explain one.
questions.solution_md: Three functions identified; one explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Pricing repairs in rupees: **measure (unit) of value**.
(ii) Being paid in cash: **medium of exchange**.
(iii) Credit sales to be paid next month: **standard of deferred payments**.
Explanation: the credit sale works because the debt is fixed **in rupees**, a unit both sides trust to have a known value when the payment falls due.

questions.stem_md: Explain any three contingent functions of money, using an imagined steel company in Jamshedpur as the example.
questions.solution_md: Three contingent functions with the company as the example.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Basis of credit**: the company's bank lends against its deposits, because loans and deposits are claims to money.
2. **Distribution of national income**: the value it produces is shared out as **wages, rent, interest and profit** in money.
3. **Liquidity and solvency**: holding money lets it **pay debts at any time**; money is the most liquid asset and shows the firm can meet its obligations.

questions.stem_md:
An imagined Hubli handloom unit sells cloth, pays weavers, borrows for looms and keeps a reserve for bad years.

(a) Explain the two primary functions of money in the unit's working. [2]
(b) Explain three secondary or contingent functions shown in the stem. [3]
questions.solution_md: Two primary functions; three further functions tied to the stem.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Medium of exchange**: cloth is sold for rupees and the same rupees buy yarn and pay weavers, so no barter is needed. **Measure of value**: cloth, yarn and wages are all priced in **rupees**, so the unit can compare costs with sales.
(b) 1. **Standard of deferred payments**: the loom loan is fixed in rupees and repaid in instalments later.
2. **Store of value**: the reserve for bad years is kept as money, which can be used whenever needed.

questions.stem_md: Explain why M1 is called narrow money and M3 broad money, as a bank officer in an imagined Kochi branch would explain to trainees.
questions.solution_md: Components of each and the liquidity reason.

answer.model_answer_md:
**M1** counts only the **most liquid** forms: **currency with the public**, **demand deposits** and **other deposits with the RBI**, all usable at once for payments, so it is **narrow money**.
**M3** adds **net time deposits** of banks to M1. Time deposits are held for a fixed period and are **less liquid**, so M3 is a **wider** measure, **broad money**.

questions.stem_md: State the meaning of M2, M3 and M4 in terms of M1, as a revision card for an imagined Shillong study group.

**M3** = M1 + **net time deposits of banks**; these fixed-period deposits make M3 a broad measure.

questions.stem_md:
An imagined finance club in Bhubaneswar is preparing a poster on money supply.

(a) Explain what is meant by money supply and whose money holdings it counts. [2]
(b) State the meaning of M1, M2, M3 and M4, and explain how their liquidity differs. [3]
questions.solution_md: Meaning and coverage; the four measures and the liquidity order.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Money supply** is the **total stock of money** held by the **public** (households and firms) at a point of time. It leaves out money held by the **government** and by the **banking system**, because that money is not available to the public for spending.
(b) **M1** = currency with the public + demand deposits + other deposits with the RBI. **M2** = M1 + savings deposits with post office savings banks. **M3** = M1 + net time deposits of banks. **M4** = M3 + total post office savings deposits (excluding National Savings Certificates). **M1** is the **most liquid**; as savings and time deposits are added, **liquidity falls**, so **M4 is the least liquid**.

marking_scheme.step: Money supply is a stock held by the public

a one-time rise in the price of onions
a rise in the money income of workers
a fall in the general price level

questions.stem_md: The price of imported crude oil rises sharply, raising transport and production costs across an imagined economy, and firms raise their prices. This is an example of

options.text_md: a fall in the purchasing power of the rupee caused by more exports

options.text_md: wage-push inflation, a form of cost-push inflation

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** profit-push inflation. Firms with market power raising margins without a rise in costs or demand push prices up: profit-push, a form of cost-push inflation.

questions.stem_md: State two causes of cost-push inflation, with an example of each from an imagined Indian manufacturing town.
questions.solution_md: Two cost-side causes with examples.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Wage-push**: a big rise in wages in the town's **lock factories** without higher productivity raises cost per lock.
2. **Rise in input prices**: dearer **imported fuel or steel** raises production costs, and firms raise prices.

questions.stem_md: Explain three causes of demand-pull inflation in an imagined economy that is already at full employment.
questions.solution_md: Three demand-side causes and the link to full employment.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Rise in money supply**, for example through easy bank credit, raises spending.
2. **Higher government spending**, especially when financed by **deficit financing** (new money), adds to aggregate demand.
3. **Rise in disposable income**, from a **tax cut** or higher exports, makes households and firms spend more.
At full employment output cannot rise, so the extra demand **pulls prices up**.

marking_scheme.step: Third cause with the full-employment link

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between demand-pull and cost-push inflation on three points, as an imagined Nagpur debate team would.
questions.solution_md: Three points of difference.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Source**: demand-pull starts from **excess demand**; cost-push starts from **rising costs** of production.
2. **Causes**: demand-pull comes from more money supply, public spending or income; cost-push from higher wages, input prices, profit margins or indirect taxes.
3. **Output**: demand-pull usually occurs **at full employment**, with output unable to rise; cost-push can occur with **idle capacity** and may even cut output.

questions.stem_md:

| Year 1 | 125 |

| Year 3 | 148.5 |

Calculate the rate of inflation in Year 2 and in Year 3, and comment on the trend.
questions.solution_md: Two rates and a comment.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Year 2**: (135 − 125) ÷ 125 × 100 = **8 per cent**.
**Year 3**: (148.5 − 135) ÷ 135 × 100 = **10 per cent**.
**Trend**: prices are rising and the **rate of inflation itself is increasing**, so the purchasing power of money is falling faster each year.

questions.stem_md:
In an imagined economy, (i) the government finances a large new road programme by borrowing from the central bank while factories already run at full capacity, and (ii) a few months later the price of imported fertiliser and diesel doubles.

(a) Identify the type of inflation in each case and explain how prices rise. [3]
(b) Explain why the second case can hurt output while the first does not raise it. [2]
questions.solution_md: Identify each type with its mechanism; contrast the effect on output.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Case (i) is **demand-pull inflation**: the road programme, paid for with **new money**, raises **aggregate demand**; since factories are at **full capacity**, output cannot rise, so buyers **bid up prices**. Case (ii) is **cost-push inflation**: dearer **fertiliser and diesel** raise the **cost of production** of food and transport, and producers **pass the higher costs on** in higher prices, even though demand has not risen.
(b) In case (i) the economy is already at **full employment**, so extra demand can only raise prices, not output. In case (ii) higher costs make some production **unprofitable**, so firms may **cut output** and jobs while prices rise.

marking_scheme.step: Case (i): no rise in output at full employment

questions.stem_md:
A family in the imagined town of Meghpur spent ₹4,000 a month on a fixed basket in the base year; the same basket now costs ₹4,600. The family's monthly income is now ₹46,000.

(a) Calculate the price index for the basket and the percentage rise in its prices. [2]
(b) Find the family's income in base-year rupees, and explain what this shows about inflation and real income. [3]
questions.solution_md: Index and inflation; real income and its meaning.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Index** = 4,600 ÷ 4,000 × 100 = **115**. **Rise in prices** = (115 − 100) ÷ 100 × 100 = **15 per cent**.
(b) **Real income** = 46,000 × 100 ÷ 115 = **₹40,000** in base-year rupees. Although the family's **money income** is ₹46,000, rising prices mean it can buy only what ₹40,000 bought in the base year. Inflation **reduces the purchasing power of money**, so a rise in money income improves living standards only if it is **faster than the rise in prices**.

marking_scheme.step: Condition for living standards to improve

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts about an imagined spice trader in Kochi. [2 + 2]

(i) She keeps part of her earnings in a fixed deposit and part in currency notes. Classify each as money or near money, with a reason.
(ii) She prices pepper in rupees and sells on three months' credit. Name the functions of money involved and explain one.
questions.solution_md: Money versus near money; two functions with one explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The **currency notes** are **money**: they are legal tender and can be **spent at once**. The **fixed deposit** is **near money**: it can be **converted into cash** quickly with little loss, but it cannot itself be **used to pay** for goods.
(ii) Pricing pepper in rupees uses money as a **measure of value**; selling on three months' credit uses money as a **standard of deferred payments**. Explanation: the debt is **fixed in rupees**, a unit both sides accept, so the buyer knows exactly what to pay when the three months are over.

marking_scheme.step: (i) Fixed deposit is near money, with reason

questions.stem_md:

(i) The consumer price index of an imagined coastal district rose from 160 to 172. Calculate the rate of inflation.
(ii) Local reports blame a big rise in the price of imported diesel used by fishing boats. Identify the type of inflation and explain how it arises.
questions.solution_md: Rate of inflation; cost-push with mechanism.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Rate of inflation** = (172 − 160) ÷ 160 × 100 = **7.5 per cent**: the general level of prices in the district has risen by that share in one year.
(ii) It is **cost-push inflation**. Diesel is a major **input** for fishing boats and for transport, so its higher price raises the **cost of catching and moving fish**. Boat owners and traders **pass the higher cost on** to buyers, so prices rise even though **demand has not increased**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts for an imagined school quiz on money supply. [2 + 2]

(i) Explain the meaning of M0 and why it is also called reserve money.
(ii) State the difference between M1 and M3, and say which is more liquid.
questions.solution_md: M0 and its name; M1 versus M3 and liquidity.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **M0** = **currency in circulation** + **bankers' deposits with the RBI** + **other deposits with the RBI**. It is called **reserve money** (or high-powered money) because the cash and deposits of banks with the central bank form the **reserves** on which banks build their lending.
(ii) **M1** = currency with the public + **demand deposits** + other deposits with the RBI, while **M3** = M1 + **net time deposits** of banks. **M1 is more liquid**, because time deposits cannot be used for payments until they mature.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [4 + 4]

(i) Trace how an imagined trading community moved from barter to commodity money, metallic coins and finally paper and bank money, explaining what each stage solved.
(ii) Explain the primary, secondary and contingent functions of money in such a community today, with one example of each kind.
questions.solution_md: Stages and what each solved; the three groups of functions with examples.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Under **barter**, trade needed a **double coincidence of wants** and had **no common measure of value**. **Commodity money** (grain, cattle, salt) gave a good that everyone accepted, but it was bulky, perishable and hard to divide. **Metallic coins** were **durable, divisible and portable**, and full-bodied coins held their value; later **token coins** saved metal. **Paper money** made large payments easy to carry, and **bank (credit) money**, moved by cheque or transfer, let traders settle big bills without cash. Each stage made exchange **cheaper and safer**.
(ii) **Primary**: money is a **medium of exchange** (a trader sells cloth for money and buys grain with it) and a **measure of value** (all goods priced in rupees). **Secondary**: a **store of value** (savings kept for the future), a **standard of deferred payments** (loans repaid later) and a **transfer of value** (selling land in one town to buy in another). **Contingent**: the **basis of credit** (banks lend against deposits), the **distribution of income** as wages, rent, interest and profit, and **liquidity**.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) Clear grouping of the three kinds

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [4 + 4]

(i) Use the price index of the imagined town of Sonapur (Year 1: 125; Year 2: 135; Year 3: 148.5) to calculate the inflation rate for Years 2 and 3 and the purchasing power of a rupee in Year 1. Explain what the figures show.
(ii) A local committee says the price rise is "all due to greedy traders". Evaluate this claim by explaining demand-pull and cost-push causes that might also be at work.
questions.solution_md: Rates, purchasing power and interpretation; balanced evaluation of causes.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Inflation in **Year 2** = (135 − 125) ÷ 125 × 100 = **8 per cent**; in **Year 3** = (148.5 − 135) ÷ 135 × 100 = **10 per cent**. In Year 1 one rupee buys **100 ÷ 125 = ₹0.8** of base-year goods. Prices are rising **faster each year**, so the **purchasing power of money is falling**, hurting people on fixed incomes.
(ii) Traders raising margins would be **profit-push** inflation, one form of cost-push, but it is unlikely to be the **only** cause. **Demand-pull** causes may be present: more **bank credit**, higher **public spending** or rising incomes can push spending above what the town produces. Other **cost-push** causes are possible too: higher **wages**, dearer **fuel and raw materials**, or higher **indirect taxes** raise costs. A fair view is that prices usually rise from **several causes together**, so the committee should study demand and costs before blaming traders alone.

questions.stem_md: Read the imagined account of a hill village and answer the questions that follow. *(Written by SOYL for practice; the village and people are imagined.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** The trader wanted rice, not oranges.

**(b)** Unit of account.

**(c) (i)** Store-of-value function.

**OR (c) (ii)** Lack of a common measure; prices in money.

answer.model_answer_md:

**(b)** Money as a **measure (unit) of value**: all sales and costs are recorded in rupees.

**OR (c) (ii)** Barter has **no common measure of value**, so every pair of goods needs its own **exchange rate**, which is hard to agree. With money, every good has a **price in rupees**, so values are easy to **compare**.

questions.stem_md: Study the imagined report on prices in Sonapur and answer the questions that follow. *(Written by SOYL for practice; the town and figures are imagined.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** (148.5 − 135) ÷ 135 × 100 = 10 per cent.

**(b)** Costs pushing prices.

**(c) (i)** Demand-pull; full capacity means prices, not output, rise.

**OR (c) (ii)** Purchasing power and its meaning.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **10%**

**(b)** **Cost-push inflation** (from dearer diesel and higher wages).

**(c) (i)** It describes **demand-pull inflation**: easy loans raise **spending**. Because workshops are at **full capacity**, output **cannot rise**, so the extra demand **pushes prices up**. The argument is reasonable, and both causes may be acting together.

**OR (c) (ii)** Purchasing power = 100 ÷ 125 = **₹0.8**: a rupee buys only what 80 paise bought in the base year. A family with a **fixed money income** can buy **less**, so its **real income falls**.

Name the type of inflation the shopkeepers describe.

answer.model_answer_md: **Cost-push inflation** (from dearer diesel and higher wages).

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Evaluate the councillor's argument: what type of inflation does it describe, and why does full capacity matter?
children.solution_md: Demand-pull; full capacity means prices, not output, rise.

answer.model_answer_md: It describes **demand-pull inflation**: easy loans raise **spending**. Because workshops are at **full capacity**, output **cannot rise**, so the extra demand **pushes prices up**. The argument is reasonable, and both causes may be acting together.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Find the purchasing power of a rupee in Year 1 (base year = 100) and explain what it means for a family with a fixed income.

answer.model_answer_md: Purchasing power = 100 ÷ 125 = **₹0.8**: a rupee buys only what 80 paise bought in the base year. A family with a **fixed money income** can buy **less**, so its **real income falls**.
